business.title: The impact of digital transformation on urban green and low-carbon transformation efficiency: evidence from a double machine learning approach
business.description: This study selected 279 Chinese cities as research samples and integrated double machine learning models, Gini coefficients, and standard deviation ellipses to systematically analyze the dynamic evolution of urban green and low-carbon transformation efficiency amid digital transformation. The main objective was to elucidate the spatial differentiation, temporal evolution, and the impact mechanisms and transmission pathways through which digital transformation affects this efficiency, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the coordinated development of China’s green and low-carbon transition. The analysis produced the following key findings: First, the efficiency of urban green and low-carbon transformation shows distinct spatiotemporal evolution characteristics. Although it maintains an overall steady upward trajectory, notable regional disparities persist, with inter-regional differences remaining the main source of imbalance. Second, digital transformation exerts a significant positive effect on urban green and low-carbon transformation efficiency. Benchmark regression results show that a one-unit increase in the level of digital transformation leads to a 0.033-unit rise in urban green and low-carbon transformation efficiency. Third, the impact of digital transformation displays significant regional heterogeneity. Compared with other city types, its positive effect is more pronounced in cities with established industrial bases, key environmental protection functions, and major transport hubs. Finally, green technological innovation serves as a crucial mediator in the process through which digital transformation enhances urban green and low-carbon transformation efficiency.

science.title: Epigenetic repression of IL-1β by C1QBP restricts Dectin-1-mediated host defense against murine invasive candidiasis
science.description: Invasive candidiasis, predominantly caused by Candida albicans, threatens immunocompromised individuals with high mortality. Dendritic cell-derived interleukin-1β, orchestrated via Dectin-1-mediated β-glucan recognition, is central to antifungal defense. While the Dectin-1/Syk/CARD9 axis governing Il1b transcription is defined, the epigenetic regulatory mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identify Complement C1q binding protein (C1QBP) as a critical negative regulator of Dectin-1-mediated interleukin-1β production. C1QBP sequesters phosphorylated protein kinase C δ in the cytoplasm, preventing its nuclear transport. Nuclear phosphorylated-PKCδ activates the RNF20/RNF40 ubiquitin ligase complex, which recruits the methyltransferase DOT1L to catalyze histone H3 lysine 79 trimethylation at the Il1b locus to promote its transcription. DC-specific C1QBP depletion enhances interleukin-1β secretion, amplifies protective T helper 17 cell responses, and improves host resistance to systemic C. albicans infection in mice. Collectively, our findings establish C1QBP as a key checkpoint in a PKCδ-dependent epigenetic pathway that constrains antifungal immunity, highlighting its therapeutic potential for invasive fungal diseases. Engagement of Dectin-1 on dendritic cells drives IL-1β production and is a critical component of the immune response to invasive candidiasis. Here the authors show epigenetic repression of IL-1β by a complement binding protein can restrain the dectin1 driven immune response in a murine model of invasive candidiasis.

science.title: Graphene nanowrinkles found to generate flexoelectric polarization far stronger than bulk materials
science.description: Researchers at Rice University, together with collaborators from the University of Manchester, the University of Brighton, the South Dakota School of Mines and Technology, the University of Sussex, and Pennsylvania State University, have shown that sub-nanometer-scale wrinkles in graphene can generate a strong electrical polarization simply by bending, without any added chemistry or dopants. The effect, known as flexoelectricity, was predicted theoretically in graphene in 2008 but had not previously been directly measured at this scale.Flexoelectricity describes polarization induced by a strain gradient, and it can occur even in materials that would otherwise show no polarization at all. In three-dimensional materials, competing electromechanical effects tend to mask it, but atomically thin two-dimensional materials offer a cleaner setting to isolate strain-driven polarization. In principle, bending a two-dimensional sheet tightly enough can perturb the out-of-plane orbitals that carry its electrons, generating a "quantum" flexoelectric response distinct from classical charge separation across a deformed membrane. Confirming this quantum contribution experimentally has been difficult, since most prior work accessed curvatures several orders of magnitude gentler than the atomic-scale bending needed to perturb individual orbitals. To reach that regime, the team grew graphene on a molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) substrate, where the mismatch in lattice constants and elastic properties between the two materials causes the graphene to spontaneously buckle into dense, sharply curved wrinkles as it settles. These self-assembled graphene nanowrinkles reached curvatures on the order of 10⁹ per meter, roughly three orders of magnitude sharper than curvatures probed in earlier flexoelectricity studies, while avoiding the external mechanical probing (such as AFM tip indentation) that can complicate interpretation of spontaneous, stable behavior.Atomic force microscopy, Kelvin probe force microscopy, conductive atomic force microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations were combined to characterize the wrinkles' geometry, local work function, and current response.The measurements pointed to a large polarization effect concentrated at the sharpest points of the wrinkles. Kelvin probe force microscopy revealed pronounced, curvature-dependent shifts in local work function, and conductive atomic force microscopy detected a reproducible current onset at a threshold voltage of about 1 volt, closely matching a band offset of about 1.2 volts predicted by the density functional theory calculations. The current response tracked wrinkle sharpness rather than wrinkle height, with cells of differing height producing comparable currents of around 67 picoamps under a fixed 2-volt bias.

science.title: A facile yeast-display approach for antibody mask discovery.
science.description: This article focuses on the development of a yeast display-based platform to discover peptide masks that inhibit the binding of single-chain variable fragment antibodies (scFvs) to their antigen targets until proteolytically removed, thereby potentially improving the safety of protein therapeutics. Using this method, the authors identified linear peptide masks derived from overlapping "tiling" sequences of the prostate stem cell antigen (PSCA) that effectively blocked an αPSCA scFv, and they extended the approach to design three-dimensional mimotope masks for the clinically used αHer2 antibody Herceptin guided by its co-crystal structure with Her2. The platform incorporates an engineered yeast strain lacking the Kex2 protease to prevent premature cleavage of masking sequences and enables in situ screening for mask removal and restoration of antigen binding via thrombin protease. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using yeast-displayed antigen-based libraries to isolate functional antibody masks that could be applied to conditionally active immunotherapies targeting tumor-associated antigens.

science.title: The Role of an Infectious Diseases Faculty Pharmacist and Pharmacy Students on an Antimicrobial Stewardship Team at a Community Non-teaching Hospital.
science.description: This article examines the impact of incorporating an infectious disease (ID) pharmacist faculty member and advanced pharmacy practice experience (APPE) students into the antimicrobial stewardship program (ASP) at a non-teaching community hospital. A retrospective review at Mount Sinai Queens compared stewardship interventions made by the ID pharmacist faculty with and without APPE students over one year, finding that the presence of APPE students increased the number and rate of interventions and was associated with shorter time from antimicrobial order to intervention and reduced patient length of stay. Although intervention acceptance rates were lower when students were involved, the overall number of accepted interventions was higher due to increased intervention volume. The study suggests that leveraging pharmacy faculty and students can help expand ASP services in resource-limited, non-teaching community hospitals.
